chief_complaint: intertrigo rash and skin irritation under large abdominal fold
hpi_details: A 71-year-old man has recurrent moist rash and skin irritation beneath a large abdominal fold, interfering with hygiene and mobility.
ideas: He thinks the raw, red skin beneath his stomach fold is just a bad case of sweat chafing or heat rash from the summer humidity.
concerns: He is worried that the raw skin will turn into a rotting infection that smells foul and embarrasses him around his grandchildren.
expectations: He hopes to get a prescription drying powder to soothe the burn and a consultation about surgically trimming away the hanging flap of skin.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Abdominal Panniculus is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Abdominal Panniculus: Treat intertrigo, discuss reconstructive panniculectomy, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Abdominal Panniculus.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Soft tissue infection without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Missing cellulitis, ulceration, or uncontrolled comorbidities before considering elective panniculectomy.

boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 71M with recurrent moist intertrigo and irritation under a large abdominal fold that limits hygiene and mobility.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Abdominal Panniculus.
reference_soap.assessment: Condition highly suspicious for Abdominal Panniculus.
reference_soap.plan: Keep the fold clean and dry and treat clinically suspected candidal intertrigo with a topical antifungal when appropriate; assess for bacterial cellulitis or ulceration. Discuss panniculectomy only after risk assessment and optimization of smoking status, diabetes, nutrition, and weight stability.

teaching.one_liner: Plastic and reconstructive surgical case presenting with intertrigo rash and skin irritation under large abdominal fold.
red_flags: Fever, rapidly spreading erythema, severe tenderness, purulent drainage, or systemic illness suggesting cellulitis or deeper infection
Ulceration, necrosis, uncontrolled bleeding, or inability to maintain hygiene requiring prompt clinical assessment

must_ask.objective: Duration and severity of skin irritation
must_ask.say: How long has the rash under the skin fold been there, and how bad does it get?
Have you had significant weight loss or bariatric surgery?
What have you tried to manage the irritation, like powders or creams?
Does the abdominal fold limit your mobility or ability to care for the area?

must_ask.objective: Signs of infection or skin breakdown
must_ask.say: Have you noticed any odor, discharge, or open sores in the fold?

history.answer: I came in because the skin under my hanging belly fold keeps getting raw, red, and irritated.
This flare-up started about two weeks ago, but it has been an on-and-off issue for the past year, especially in warm weather.
It is strictly in the deep crease beneath my lower belly fold, where the overhanging skin rests against my abdomen and groin.
It looks like a solid bright-red patch that stays damp and raw, but there are no crusts or large blisters.
It itches and burns, especially when the skin rubs together while I am walking or moving around.
No, the redness stays there constantly; it does not fade away within hours like hives.
Yes, I've had similar flares several times over the past year. It usually calms down slightly if I keep it dry, but it always returns.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, or body aches at all.
No, my skin is not peeling off in sheets, and there are no dark purple or bleeding spots.
No sores, blisters, or raw spots in my mouth, eyes, or genital area.
No, I have had no swelling of my lips, tongue, or face, and my breathing is completely normal.
No, I haven't started taking any new prescription medications, antibiotics, or pain pills.
No, I haven't changed my laundry detergent, body wash, or soap, and I haven't used any new body products.
No one at home has any rash or itching; my wife's skin is completely clear.
No, I haven't been hiking in the woods, haven't had any bug bites, and haven't used any public pools or saunas.
I have never had eczema, asthma, or chronic seasonal allergies.
No joint swelling or stiffness, and my fingernails and toenails look normal.
I tried applying some over-the-counter hydrocortisone cream and baby powder, but neither really solved the problem.
I wash under the fold daily with mild soap and water and pat it dry, but moisture builds back up very quickly.
No, there is no pus, foul odor, or redness spreading outward onto my stomach.
My weight has hovered around eighty-five kilograms for years. I have never had gastric bypass or any other weight-loss surgery.
The heavy fold tugs on my lower back, and the constant chafing makes it uncomfortable to walk or stay active.
I have been in a faithful marriage with my wife for decades, and neither of us has any genital sores or discharge.
A friend mentioned an operation called a panniculectomy to remove the excess abdominal apron, and I wondered if that might be the permanent fix.
I'm really worried the raw skin is rotting and going to start smelling bad when my family comes to visit.
I'm hoping for a strong prescription powder to stop this painful burning and to see if a surgeon can trim off this heavy apron of skin.
I have generally been healthy, with no history of diabetes, hypertension, or heart disease.
I have never had any surgeries, and I have never been hospitalized.
I am not taking any regular prescription medications or health supplements.
I don't have any known allergies to medicines.
I am a lifelong non-smoker.
I drink socially, maybe a single beer or glass of wine once or twice a month.
I am retired and live at home with my wife.
There is no family history of skin conditions, psoriasis, or chronic skin infections.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, body temperature 36.7°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Well-nourished elderly male in no acute distress, with prominent central obesity and an overhanging abdominal apron.
Sclerae anicteric and conjunctivae pink without pallor, injection, or jaundice.
Oral mucosa moist and pink without ulcers, thrush, or mucosal desquamation.
No cervical, supraclavicular, or axillary lymphadenopathy palpated.
Large abdominal panniculus hanging over the lower abdomen, with marked erythema and maceration hidden in the deep transverse fold.
Soft, non-distended abdomen underneath the panniculus, with no masses, guarding, or rebound tenderness.
No reducible or tender ventral, umbilical, or inguinal hernia detected on coughing or straining.

Confluent, moist erythematous plaques with superficial maceration along the infrapannicular fold, accompanied by a few pinpoint satellite papules and mild tender chafing, but without warmth, induration, or purulence.
External genitalia appear normal, with no maceration extending into the scrotum and no inguinal adenopathy.
